World's Big Game Hunters Dread London Traffic.
TIMID LION SLAYERS.
Thirty timid-looking men crossed Piccadilly traffic in safety last night on their way to the Criterion Restaurant—thanks to the aid of policemen.

The thirty-first man, a vigorous person, dashed fearlessly through to the same destination, and afterwards all assembled in a private dining-room, where the annual dinner of the Ju Ja Club was held under the chairmanship of Mr. Granville Kay.
It then appeared that the intrepid, vigorous person was a railway official, while the thirty who shrank from the horrors of West End traffic
Mr. F. C. Selous, with Ju Ja.
were world-famous big-game hunters, each of whom counted scores, and in some cases hundreds, of lions and elephants to his credit in the jungles of East and Central Africa.

The Club Ju Ja was formed of those who had been guests of Mr. William M. McMillan, the American sportsman, a pioneer of East-Africa, whose shooting preserve near Nairobi, on which he expended £80,000, is named Ju Ja.
BACK FROM CONGO.
Ju Ja is a West African god who in wooden form was present at the founding of the farm, and was last night at the dinner, though the host at the last minute, unhappily, was unable to attend.
These thirty-one men met, some of them, for the first time in many years.
At the head table was F. C. Selous, the record elephant killer. By his side sat the beardless youth, Quentin Grogan, just back from the Congo, who ranks second to Selous in elephant killing.

Hidden between Mr. Grogan and the next guest was an undersized, bashful man. This was Mr. John Boyce, the white King of the Ki-ku-yus, a romantic figure in Central African history. He seemed afraid to speak or to move.

Yet this man as a boy—shipwrecked on the shores of East Africa, with only his bare fists for weapons—fought his way inland, and became the recognised king of the savage Ki-ku-yus, a tribe numbering 4,000,900.
Mr. Boyce has lately been shooting elephants in the Congo. He killed 150 in a few months.
Then there was Mr. Hugh Heatley, who has a long list of lion "kills" to his credit, and whose farm furnished Mr. Roosevelt his finest buffaloes in Africa.

APRIL 8.—Bulbs are flowering so early this year that beds filled with them will be able to be cleared soon for summer flowers. Tulips and hyacinths, when past their best, should be carefully lifted and planted close together in an odd corner to complete their growth. Give them a good watering. By the middle of July the foliage will have faded and the bulbs can then be dug up.

Narcissi, if possible, ought not to be disturbed. It is a good plan to sow some free-growing annuals around them; then, when the foliage of the narcissi is dead, the beds will be gay again. The leaves of crocuses and other bulbs growing in the grass must not be cut or there will be little bloom next year. E. F. T.

The Press Club entertained on Saturday night, at their monthly house dinner, Sir William Treloar, the Lord Mayor of London, who has been a member of the club for many years. Taking advantage of the fact that he was one of themselves, they "ragged" him most unmercifully.
"I have never been ragged so much before in my life," he said to the Daily Mirror as he drove home. "And I enjoyed it, I may tell you, more than anything I have attended for months."

Scarcely had the Lord Mayor sat down to dinner than the members of the Bottom Table, who, consisting as they do of the more youthful and noisy members of the club, are allowed almost unlimited licence, interrupted the proceedings with a mock Lord Mayor's Show. Then the mock Recorder recited a mock ode, which was engraved on parchment and sealed with a huge wax seal embossed with the likeness of the one-eyed Press Club cat. The ode was afterwards presented to the Lord Mayor in a magnificent casket—a brand-new wastepaper basket.

When these preliminary proceedings had terminated the dinner was allowed to go on for a while, but before long the Lord Mayor was dragged down to the Bottom Table and made to drink the healths of the noisy Pressmen who sat there. When the dinner was over the Recorder again approached his lordship and recited another long poem, in which he declared the members' intention of investing the Lord Mayor:—

'Mid dreadful oaths beneath this solemn gable, With the full freedom of the Bottom Table. For this great decoration kings have sighed, For such an honour rajahs would have died, For this small scrap of stamped and cherished vellum The cerebrum and e'en the cerebellum Of belted earls have ached and ached again, But they have always ached, my lord, in vain. This is the uttered oath while lights burn blue, In deepest sorrecy, Lord Mayor, to you.

Then gongs were banged, lights were turned down, blue flames emitted from the curtain room in which the Bottom Table is placed, and the Lord Mayor swore a fearfully mysterious oath, and was presented with the parchment bearing the freedom which had been conferred upon him.

When the dinner was over the Lord Mayor refused to accept the ode unless it was enclosed in the wastepaper-basket in which it had been presented. For nearly half an hour the Lord Mayor's coachman had to wait while the "casket" was being found. But as it was ultimately discovered that one of the members of the Bottom Table had sat on the basket, the Lord Mayor will not receive his ode until a fresh one has been bought.

J. WOOD, THE FAMOUS MUSICIAN, IN THE DUAL ROLE OF CONDUCTOR AND PAINTER.

Until this week, when an exhibition of his oil paintings was opened at the Piccadilly Arcade Gallery; few people knew that Sir Henry J. Wood, the famous conductor, was also a painter. Despite the fact that the London musical festival, of which he is conductor, has made him tremendously busy, he has found time to arrange for this display of his skill in another branch of art. It was indeed his first

love, for as a young man he studied painting and drawing, but the claim of music proved too strong, and he adopted it as a career. He has not, however, entirely abandoned the brush for the baton, as he finds painting a pleasant relaxation. The photographs, taken yesterday, show (1) Sir Henry conducting. (2) Mixing his colours.
